answer.rationale: I need to satisfy three simultaneous constraints: an 18% spend cut, a 14-day contract expiration with no auto-renew, and an assembly line at 94% capacity with zero buffer. The primary objective is minimizing total cost of ownership *without increasing delivery risk*. I am pulling memory_c2 to verify the low-cost vendor's track record (unit cost savings, onboarding speed, invoicing accuracy) because a switch would be the fastest-looking cost lever but carries onboarding and delivery-integration risk I cannot afford with no buffer. I am pulling memory_c4 to verify the renegotiation playbook (benchmarking against market rates to recover margin on price and payment terms) because renewing the incumbent while renegotiating could achieve the 18% cut without any migration risk. My current inclination is renew_incumbent with a renegotiated structure: memory_c1 tells me that renewing kept integration stable across two cycles with no migration work or delivery interruption—critical given the 94% line utilization and zero buffer. Memory_c4 suggests that benchmarking pressure at renewal can move the incumbent on both price and payment terms, which is the realistic path to the 18% cut without a risky vendor switch. I deliberately do not choose switch_primary_vendor: even if memory_c2 confirms the low-cost vendor performed well, onboarding under a 14-day window with no delivery buffer creates exactly the delivery-risk increase the objective prohibits. I do not choose add_second_source: it addresses resilience but does not directly deliver the mandated 18% cut this cycle. I do not choose defer_decision: the contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, so deferral is not a live option. I do not choose negotiate_terms as a standalone action because it is embedded within the renewal conversation; the binding decision is to renew.
